title: Groups, periods and periodic trends
blurb: Name the main element families and predict atomic radius, ionization energy, electronegativity and reactivity from position.
question: Two elements sit in the same period: sodium on the far left and chlorine near the far right. Which has the larger atoms, which holds its electrons more tightly, and why?

teach.body: Formally, a periodic trend is a regular change in a property as you move across a period or down a group. In plain English: once you know where an element sits, you can predict its size, how tightly it holds electrons and how it reacts, without memorizing each element. Two ideas drive every trend: how many protons are pulling, and how many shells the electrons sit in.

head: Group
Family
Key facts
rows: 1 valence e⁻; +1 ions; most reactive metals; react vigorously with water
7 valence e⁻; −1 ions; most reactive nonmetals; diatomic (F₂, Cl₂)
teach.caption: Hydrogen sits at the top of group 1 but is a nonmetal, not an alkali metal.

teach.body: Across a period, each element adds a proton while the electrons stay in the same number of shells. The stronger positive pull draws the shells in: atoms get smaller, harder to strip (higher ionization energy) and greedier for shared electrons (higher electronegativity). Down a group, each element adds a whole shell. Outer electrons sit farther out, so atoms get larger and hold them less tightly.

teach.caption: Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron. Electronegativity is an atom's pull on shared electrons in a bond.
Radius shrinks left to right while ionization energy and electronegativity climb.

teach.body: A cation is smaller than its parent atom: losing electrons (often a whole outer shell) lets the nucleus pull the rest closer, so Na⁺ is smaller than Na. An anion is larger than its parent atom: extra electrons repel each other and spread out, so Cl⁻ is larger than Cl. Seven elements exist naturally as two-atom molecules: H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂.

teach.caption: Say it 'hoff-brinkle'. The noble gases are never diatomic: they exist as single atoms.

teach.h: Scenario: Aaliyah ranks the alkali metals
teach.body: Aaliyah, preparing for her TEAS, must rank lithium, sodium and potassium by how vigorously they react with water. All three are group 1, each with one valence electron to lose. Going down the group adds shells, so the valence electron sits farther from the nucleus and is lost more easily (lower ionization energy). Her ranking, least to most reactive: lithium, sodium, potassium.

teach.text: Atomic radius DECREASES left to right (more protons, same shells), even though the atoms are getting heavier. Electronegativity is highest at the TOP RIGHT (fluorine), not the bottom left. And noble gases are inert, not highly reactive.

items: Group 1 alkali metals and group 17 halogens are the most reactive families; group 18 noble gases are inert.
Across a period: radius down; ionization energy and electronegativity up; metallic character down.
Down a group: radius up; ionization energy and electronegativity down; metallic character up.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element; cesium and francium are the least.
Cations are smaller than their atoms; anions are larger. Diatomic: H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂.

summary: You can now name the main families of the periodic table and predict how atomic radius, ionization energy, electronegativity and metallic character change across a period and down a group. You can also compare ion sizes and list the diatomic elements.

A.q: Which group contains the most reactive nonmetals?
A.why: The halogens (group 17) have 7 valence electrons and need just one more, making them the most reactive nonmetals.

whyNot.0: Alkali metals are the most reactive METALS, not nonmetals.
whyNot.2: Noble gases have a full outer shell and are very unreactive.
whyNot.3: Alkaline earth metals are metals that form +2 ions.

A.q: Moving from left to right across period 3, what happens to atomic radius?
A.why: Each step adds a proton but no new shell, so the stronger pull draws the electrons closer and the atoms shrink.

whyNot.0: Radius increases DOWN a group (new shells), not across a period.
whyNot.1: The shell count stays the same, but the rising nuclear charge does shrink the atoms.
whyNot.2: There is no rise-then-fall pattern; the radius shrinks steadily across the period.

A.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity?
A.why: Fluorine, at the top right of the table (excluding noble gases), has the strongest pull on shared electrons.

whyNot.1: Chlorine is below fluorine in group 17; electronegativity falls down a group.
whyNot.2: Cesium, at the bottom left, is among the least electronegative elements.
whyNot.3: Noble gases such as helium are usually left out of electronegativity scales because they rarely bond.

B.q: Why does atomic radius increase down a group?
options: Each step adds a new shell
B.why: Each step down a group adds a new occupied shell, so the outer electrons sit farther from the nucleus.

whyNot.0: Protons increase going down a group, not decrease.
whyNot.1: Members of a group have the same number of valence electrons.
whyNot.3: Nuclear charge rises down a group; the extra shells outweigh it.

B.q: Which ion is larger than the neutral atom it formed from?
B.why: Cl⁻ is an anion: the extra electron increases repulsion and the electron cloud spreads out, so it is larger than Cl.

whyNot.1: Na⁺ is a cation; losing its outer electron makes it smaller than Na.
whyNot.2: Mg²⁺ has lost its outer shell, so it is smaller than Mg.
whyNot.3: Ca²⁺ is a cation and is smaller than the Ca atom.

B.why: Potassium is below sodium in group 1; its valence electron is farther out and lost more easily, so it reacts more vigorously.

whyNot.0: Ionization energy decreases down a group, so potassium's is lower.
whyNot.1: Potassium has an extra shell, so its radius is larger.
whyNot.2: Electronegativity decreases down a group, so potassium's is lower.

C.q: Which list places the elements in order of INCREASING first ionization energy?
C.why: All three are in period 3. Ionization energy rises left to right: Na (group 1) < Mg (group 2) < Cl (group 17).

whyNot.0: This is decreasing order: chlorine, on the right, has the highest ionization energy.
whyNot.2: Magnesium is to the right of sodium, so its ionization energy is higher, not lower.
whyNot.3: Chlorine is farthest right, so it belongs last (highest), after magnesium.

C.q: In a demonstration, lithium fizzes steadily in water and sodium darts around rapidly. What should the class predict for potassium?
options: Slower, because it has more protons
Slower, because its ionization energy is higher
Faster, because its outer electron is farther out
About the same, because all have one valence electron
C.why: Down group 1 the valence electron sits in a higher shell, farther from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily and the reaction is more vigorous.

whyNot.0: More protons are outweighed by the extra shell; reactivity of metals increases down a group.
whyNot.1: Ionization energy decreases down a group, so potassium's is lower, not higher.
whyNot.3: Sharing one valence electron explains why they react alike, but reactivity still rises down the group.

C.q: Which statement about metallic character is correct?
options: It is highest at the top right
C.why: Metallic character (the tendency to lose electrons) rises down a group as outer electrons sit farther out.

whyNot.1: Metallic character decreases across a period as atoms hold electrons more tightly.
whyNot.2: Group 17 holds the halogens, the most reactive nonmetals.
whyNot.3: The top right is the most nonmetallic region; the most metallic is the bottom left.

reteach.title: Magnets and distance
reteach.question: Hold a paperclip near a magnet, then farther away, then near a stronger magnet. How does that explain every periodic trend?

blocks.body: The nucleus is a magnet and the outer electrons are paperclips. Going across a period turns up the magnet's strength (more protons) while the paperclips stay the same distance away (same shells): they are pulled in tighter, so atoms shrink and grip harder. Going down a group moves the paperclips farther away (new shells): the grip weakens, atoms swell and lose electrons more easily.

blocks.h: Turn a dial, see the effect

blocks.text: Heavier does not mean bigger. Chlorine has more mass than sodium, yet its atoms are smaller because its stronger nucleus pulls the same three shells closer.

explain.body: Group 1 alkali metals (1 valence e⁻, most reactive metals), group 2 alkaline earth metals (+2 ions), groups 3 to 12 transition metals, group 17 halogens (7 valence e⁻, most reactive nonmetals) and group 18 noble gases (full shell, inert).

test.q: An element is a colorless gas whose atoms have a full outer shell and almost never form compounds. Which group is it in?
test.why: A full outer shell and almost no reactivity describe the noble gases, group 18.

whyNot.0: Group 1 alkali metals are highly reactive solids with one valence electron.
whyNot.1: Group 2 alkaline earth metals are reactive metals that form +2 ions.
whyNot.2: Halogens are one electron short of a full shell, making them highly reactive.

explain.body: Protons increase but the shell count stays the same, so the pull on outer electrons strengthens. Radius falls; ionization energy and electronegativity rise; metallic character falls.

test.q: Electronegativity increases across a period mainly because:
options: more protons pull on the same shells
the atoms lose their valence electrons
test.why: Across a period the nuclear charge rises while electrons stay in the same shells, so the atom pulls shared electrons harder.

whyNot.0: The shell count stays the same across a period; it rises down a group.
whyNot.2: Atoms on the right tend to gain electrons, not lose them.
whyNot.3: Neutrons carry no charge and do not explain the trend; the rising proton count does.

explain.body: Each step down adds a shell. Outer electrons are farther away, so radius rises; ionization energy and electronegativity fall; metals become more reactive.

test.q: Which of these group 1 elements has the lowest first ionization energy?
test.why: Ionization energy decreases down a group; cesium is lowest of these, with its valence electron farthest from the nucleus.

whyNot.0: Lithium is near the top of group 1, so it has a high ionization energy for the group.
whyNot.1: Sodium is above cesium, so its outer electron is held more tightly.
whyNot.3: Hydrogen's single electron sits right next to the nucleus, so it is hard to remove.

explain.body: Cations are smaller than their atoms; anions are larger. Seven elements exist as two-atom molecules: H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ (HOFBrINCl).

test.q: Which element exists naturally as diatomic molecules?
test.why: Nitrogen gas is N₂, one of the seven diatomic elements (HOFBrINCl).

whyNot.1: Neon is a noble gas and exists as single atoms.
whyNot.2: Sodium is a metal held together by metallic bonding, not as Na₂ molecules.
whyNot.3: Phosphorus is not on the diatomic list (HOFBrINCl), so it does not exist as P₂ molecules.
